misconceptions.constant-inside-log: The constant multiplies the log; it doesn't go inside it. (ln|cx|)′ = 1/x, not c/x.
misconceptions.differentiated-a: Velocity is the antiderivative of acceleration, not its derivative.
misconceptions.differentiated-instead: That's the derivative. An antiderivative goes the other way: its derivative should give back the original.
misconceptions.divided-by-old-exponent: Divide by the new exponent, n + 1, not the old one: then differentiating gives back the original coefficient.
misconceptions.divided-not-raised: Raise the exponent by one as well as dividing: the antiderivative of xⁿ is xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1).
misconceptions.forgot-to-divide: Raising the power isn't enough: divide by the new exponent, so differentiating brings the coefficient back.
misconceptions.forgot-v0: Integrating gives a constant too: here it's the starting velocity v(0).
misconceptions.integrated-twice: That integrates the acceleration twice. Velocity needs one integration; position needs two.
misconceptions.multiplied-by-k: Differentiating sin(kx) brings out a factor k, so the antiderivative of cos(kx) must divide by k, not multiply.
misconceptions.multiplied-by-n: Multiplying by the new exponent is what differentiating does. To undo it, divide.
misconceptions.position-not-velocity: That's the shape of the position formula. Velocity needs only one integration of the acceleration.
misconceptions.power-rule-on-exp: e^{kx} isn't x to a power, so the power rule doesn't apply. Undo the chain rule: divide by k.
misconceptions.power-rule-on-trig: sec² isn't a power of a variable. Read the derivative table backwards: (tan x)′ = sec² x.
misconceptions.sin-sign: (cos x)′ = −sin x, so the antiderivative of sin x is −cos x: the minus sign comes along.
